description: Equipo para que necesiten datos y UX.
summary:
We developed Know Your Farm, a Python and Streamlit decision-support web which translates NASA Earth observation datasets (POWER, SMAP, MODIS, and ECOSTRESS) into parcel-level insights across four views: an interactive geospatial map (pydeck) with historical scrubbing, a field diagnostic dashboard tracking bare-soil and climate hazards, a crop-rotation simulator with climate stress sliders, and a personalized action-plan engine. It also features Mr. Corn, a Gemini-powered agronomy assistant querying farm metrics via function calling.

The platform operationalizes four pillars: comparing multi-season crop rotations, revealing ecological and economic tradeoffs, quantifying plot risks, and displaying model uncertainty via 90% confidence intervals.

Global food security relies directly on local farm resilience, agricultural disruptions in major producers like the U.S. ripple across interconnected supply chains in countries like Mexico and beyond. While this prototype uses U.S. datasets, its satellite-driven architecture is built to scale worldwide. By pairing NASA data with farmer priorities, while flagging data gaps for local verification. Know Your Farm empowers growers everywhere to sustain the food systems we all depend on.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

We developed Know Your Farm, a Python and Streamlit decision-support web application that translates NASA Earth observations (POWER, MODIS) and USDA agricultural datasets into parcel-level insights for 167 real agricultural fields in Butler County, Iowa. The platform is organized around four interactive views:

Interactive geospatial map: Built with Leaflet and GeoJSON field geometries derived from the USDA Cropland Data Layer, it lets growers inspect individual fields over aerial or terrain basemaps, toggle soil layers including productivity, sand content, slope-driven erosion risk and planting-time flood risk, and view a national context layer of roughly 16 million U.S. field polygons with their 2025 crop.

Field diagnostic dashboard: Shows each field’s eight-year rotation history, its stored water, sand, slope and organic matter, the yield adjustment its soil implies, and its measured risk of not being plantable in a wet spring.

Crop-rotation simulator: Evaluates rotations across three historical climate regimes — normal, dry-and-hot, and wet-spring — derived from 26 years of measured NASA POWER climate rather than from past yields. Users compare continuous corn, corn-soybean, and corn-soybean with a winter cover crop, seeing both the harvest and the money side by side.

Personalized action-plan engine: Turns the chosen plan into a short checklist covering budget, soil protection, nitrogen and risk, while flagging the data gaps that require on-farm verification.

Across all four views the platform operationalizes the four pillars of the challenge: comparing multi-season rotations, revealing ecological and economic tradeoffs, quantifying plot-level risk, and displaying uncertainty as an 80% range — the 10th to the 90th percentile of 26 historical years. It also features Mr. Corn, a Gemini-powered agronomy assistant that queries live parcel metrics, climate regimes and rotation tradeoffs through structured function calling rather than guessing numbers.

What benefits does it have?

Know Your Farm bridges the gap between raw orbital datasets and practical field-level planning:

Clear economic and environmental tradeoffs: Instead of looking at yield in isolation, growers see expected corn yield (bu/acre) and net margin (USD/acre) right next to soil erosion (ton/acre/year) and the nitrogen the plan requires (lb/acre). Our own analysis is why both are always shown: in 2012 Butler County harvested 34% less corn than expected, yet prices rose so sharply that income ended 17% above average. A tool reporting only bushels would have called that the farmer’s worst year.

Uncertainty that was tested, not asserted: Many agricultural tools show a single number as if future weather were guaranteed. We show an 80% range and we verified it by leaving each year out of the fit: a range promising to cover 80% of cases covered exactly 80%, and a 90% range covered 89%.

Risk the soil survey missed: In 2019, 2,293 acres in the county went unplanted. We measure this per field from satellite imagery. The official soil survey’s flooding rating did not predict which fields were affected — the correlation is effectively zero — while the satellite record did. Three fields exceed 5% unplanted area, with a maximum of 46%.

Tradeoffs that are honest about cost: A winter cover crop costs about $37 per acre to establish. On good flat ground that turns a positive margin negative while cutting erosion by 60%; on steep ground it stays profitable and saves 8.4 tons of soil per acre per year. The same practice gives different answers on different fields, and the tool says so.

Plain-language guidance: Growers do not need remote-sensing expertise to interpret NDVI or root-zone moisture. Visual diagnostics and Mr. Corn translate those metrics into straightforward field summaries, while noting where local soil tests or drainage checks are still needed.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Global food security relies directly on local farm resilience. Agricultural disruptions in major producers like the U.S. ripple across interconnected supply chains in countries like Mexico and beyond, affecting grain availability, feed costs, and food prices for millions of households.

This prototype uses U.S. datasets from Butler County, Iowa, but the model was deliberately built on variables that exist nationwide: NASA POWER has global coverage, USDA QuickStats covers every U.S. county, SSURGO covers the country, and the Cropland Data Layer covers the contiguous states. Moving to another county means changing the input files, not rewriting the model. By pairing NASA Earth observations with on-the-ground agronomic literature, and by flagging every gap that needs local verification, Know Your Farm helps growers adapt to hotter, drier and more erratic growing seasons.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Programming languages: Python for the core application, data pipelines, agronomic modeling and test suites, alongside JavaScript, HTML and CSS for custom interactive map and interface components, plus JSON and GeoJSON for structured spatial and model outputs.

Frameworks and libraries: Streamlit for the web interface and state management, Leaflet and pydeck for interactive map rendering, google-genai for Gemini function calling in Mr. Corn, and pandas, numpy, scipy, rasterio and geopandas for aligning multi-source raster and vector data and computing the empirical percentile ranges.

NASA and agricultural datasets: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) for daily temperature, precipitation and root-zone soil wetness; NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 via AppEEARS for NDVI vegetation dynamics; USDA NASS QuickStats for county yields, planted area and prices; USDA NRCS SSURGO for soil properties; and the USDA Cropland Data Layer for the crop planted on every 30 m pixel, from which our field polygons were derived. NASA NLDAS-2 soil moisture was examined during analysis and supported the wet-spring interpretation.

Agronomic literature: Iowa State University for production costs, the continuous-corn yield penalty, nitrogen rate guidance and cover crop economics.

AI development and runtime tools: Claude Code and Codex were used throughout development for coding, refactoring and validation, while the Google Gemini API powers Mr. Corn’s tool-grounded responses inside the live app.

Testing, version control and hardware: Automated offline verification built with Python’s unittest framework and Node.js (node:test with jsdom), Git and GitHub for version control, and standard developer laptops running local Python environments.

How is your project creative?

Most farm software either overwhelms users with dense agronomic spreadsheets or presents black-box recommendations without explaining why a strategy works or where it might fail. Know Your Farm takes a different approach in three ways:

Building humility into the interface: Instead of pretending satellite pixels tell the whole story of a field, our system surfaces uncertainty through tested 80% ranges and declares what it could not measure. The clearest example is on screen: we tried four different ways to measure the continuous-corn yield penalty from county data and all of them failed our falsification tests, so that number comes from Iowa State literature and the app says so rather than hiding it. Where a value does not exist, the interface shows “Not available” instead of a plausible-looking number.

Connecting orbital data to conversational tool calling: Rather than embedding a generic chatbot that gives vague farming tips, we wired Mr. Corn directly into the app’s session state via function calling. When a grower switches fields or changes the climate regime, Mr. Corn inspects those exact numbers before answering.

Side-by-side ecological accounting: Putting net income per acre directly beside soil erosion and nitrogen requirement reframes crop rotation from a single-season yield bet into a multi-year resilience decision.

What factors did your team consider?

Aligning datasets that do not share a grid: The Cropland Data Layer is a 30 m raster in Albers projection, MODIS NDVI is 250 m in geographic coordinates, and SSURGO is vector polygons. Bringing them onto one grid without smearing the boundaries was the central technical problem, and sub-field variability remains a caveat we state to the user.

Verifying every finding a second way: After each result we re-tested it from a different angle. That discipline changed several conclusions. We believed poor drainage was the county’s main soil limitation until an area-weighted analysis showed the opposite — poorly drained Iowa soils are among the most productive because they are tile-drained, and the real limit is sand. We also found that an earlier version of our own flood-risk finding did not reproduce, and we replaced it with the measured result.

Scientific guardrails and unit consistency: Mixing units or letting an AI assistant invent commodity prices would quickly break trust with real growers. All conversions between agricultural units (bu/acre, USD/acre, ton/acre/year, lb/acre) and the application’s internal metric contract pass through a single module, and the assistant reports only values present in the active model context.

Balancing soil health with farm economics: A rotation that halves erosion will not be adopted if it leaves a farm with negative cash flow. At current prices, 94 of our 167 fields have no profitable plan at all, so the tool states plainly that the useful question for those growers is which plan loses least.

Cross-border food chain connections and global portability: Because weather shocks in U.S. grain-producing states affect supply chains in Mexico and other trading partners, we avoided hardcoding U.S.-only assumptions into the model, keeping it ready for international adaptation.
